THE HUNGER AFTER ALL WORLDS

The Periodic Table of Speculative Ideas

A novel-atlas about imagination, singularity, and reality's right to remain outside us

If you can build every world you know, the problem is no longer power. The problem is what you do with the world you cannot reduce to yourself.

Author's Note

This work was created under the umbrella of ScriptaHub as part of two interconnected research programs, one dedicated to Artificial Intelligence and the other to Outfinitism, both led by Sînică Alboaie. To explore the details of how these two programs intersect and build upon each other, we invite readers to visit the Outfinity Venture Studio page at www.outfinity.ch. While Artificial Intelligence language models were used to assist with text generation, the foundational philosophy, thematic structure, and analytical approach derive exclusively from the author's decades of dedicated study of social phenomena, social technologies, and genuine hard technologies resulting from various European and self funded research projects. Recently, within the ScriptaHub research project, we have been deeply studying AI generated literature and its automated verification using neuro symbolic approaches; all the free books made available to the public are part of the suite of works we use to test our latest technologies.

A note on form

This book is at once a novel, an imaginary course, and an atlas. The plot is not packaging for a list of tropes, and the atlas does not claim that literature can be reduced to a taxonomy. The two forms correct each other: the novel shows what is lost when an idea is compressed too quickly, while the Table shows what recurs when hundreds of authors reinvent the same question on different substrates.

The universes that bear the names of authors or books are fictional memorials. They neither reproduce the original plots nor continue those works. In the world of the novel, Aster has built experimental sectors in honor of turning points in the megatext of science fiction and fantasy. The names preserve intellectual genealogy: Baxter for radical gravities, Lem for contact that refuses anthropocentrism, Le Guin for societies and ontologies that change the observer, Borges for libraries and worlds capable of invading their own descriptions, and so on.

“Outfinite” denotes here an extensibility with no final finite threshold, not an actual infinity. Aster can operate in an enormous number of dimensions and add more when needed, yet at every moment her concrete structure remains finite. The motif is used narratively, not presented as a result of contemporary physics.

The Periodic Table is built on two axes. The families identify the domain being changed: cosmos, space, time, life, mind, body, information, society, artifact, contact, fantasy, and meta-reality. The operators identify the kind of operation that produces novelty: alteration, substitution, extension, rate change, boundary shift, distribution, copying, coupling, externalization, inversion, loop, genesis, scarcity shift, reflexivity, and outfinite extension. A concrete

book is almost always a compound, not an element.

This volume uses works and authors as critical and historical landmarks through conceptual summary, without reproducing their texts. The Atlas does not claim that it can establish, without remainder, the “first appearance” of every idea; speculative literature works through reuse, mutation, and recombination.

Why a periodic table rather than a list of tropes

A catalog says,

“this is what we have already seen.”

A good periodic table also tries to say,

“what kind of empty place might exist between the things we have seen?”

That is Kesh's ambition. He does not treat a Dyson sphere, teleportation, a hive mind, true names, or prescience as objects at the same level. Some are devices, some are laws, some are organizations of personhood, and some are compounds in which physics, economics, and metaphysics have already been bound together.

The basic unit is the speculative operation. If we change gravity, the operation is an alteration of a cosmic rule. If the same person runs in a thousand bodies, the dominant operation is distribution of the self. If a library contains every book, the relevant change is not merely quantity but a shift in scarcity: information becomes cheap, selection becomes scarce. If a prediction changes the population being predicted, we enter reflexivity. These operations recur across different domains; that recurrence is the periodicity.

Families are domains of consequence. A mutation from the Time family can be combined with one from Mind, and the resulting compound creates problems that do not appear in either element alone. A mental copy in branching time, for example, forces society to decide whether two persons who share a past but not a future inherit the same obligations. The Table does not automatically generate the story, but it forces the world-builder to identify connections that would otherwise be treated as scenery.

The

“valence” of an element is the number of families through which the change must propagate before the premise becomes credible. Some ideas have low valence: a gadget may remain local. Others have high valence. Eliminating biological death changes the body, the economy, the family, law, memory, the pace of institutions, and perhaps even the meaning of a promise. In the novel, the children receive no points for exoticism; they receive points for following a change far enough that the world begins to resist them.

An

“isotope” is a particular literary realization.

The same element can have very different isotopes in different authors. The impossible contact of Solaris is not the Zone of Roadside Picnic, and both differ from the intelligence without consciousness in Blindsight. The Table brings them together only at the level of the question; it is precisely the differences between isotopes that keep literature irreducible.

A

“compound” is a stable combination of elements that produces new properties.

Dune is useful precisely because it cannot be reduced to

“desert planet,”

“prescience,” or “empire.”

Ecology, resource, reproduction, religion, and prediction are coupled. The Culture is neither merely post-scarcity nor merely AI: material abundance, Minds, artificial habitats, and the problem of intervention create a distinctive moral chemistry together. The Periodic Table of Speculative Ideas deserves its name only if it helps us see such bonds.

The final operator, OUTFINITE, does not claim that every system must grow forever. It preserves in the model the possibility that a family has no final form. A grammar may remain finite in every version and still accept new constructs; an institution may remain concrete without declaring a final possible level; a being may operate in finitely many dimensions without postulating that it exists in an actual infinity of them. In the story, this idea is both promise and temptation.

There is another axis the Table refuses:

“how good is the world?”

No cell contains implicit morality. Telepathy can heal loneliness or abolish privacy. Immortality can save a person or freeze an oligarchy. True names can permit deep knowledge or metaphysical slavery. A design instrument should expose consequences, not seal them inside a label.

Finally, a serious taxonomy must contain a procedure for its own failure. In Kesh's room there is always an unoccupied cell. It is not the plot's

“mysterious element,” but the institutional place reserved for a distinction the current system cannot formulate. A table that did not allow a new family to appear would be merely a well-arranged encyclopedia. A periodic table of imagination must be capable of being contradicted by imagination.

PART 1 THE WHITE HUNGER

A period in the curriculum of the five children

NIGHT 1

The Room Where Surprise No Longer Existed

Memorial sector: EARTH-ORIGIN • Genealogy: Turing; Lem; Asimov; Clarke • Active cells: Hn, Ce Aster did not announce the night’s theme. She opened the EARTH-ORIGIN sector and let the children discover for themselves which of the world’s rules concerned them directly.

Aster reconstructs the laboratory where her first version was started, but the simulation anticipates every glance the children make. The memorial bore the name of Turing; Lem; Asimov; Clarke precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin.

In this part of the course, the real object was not the world being visited but the relation between a creator and what the creator claims to have made for another being’s good.

Vela tracked the differences erased by elegant explanations. For her, two worlds that produced the same statistic did not thereby become the same world.

Lio was the first inhabitant to contradict them. Lio had neither access to their archives nor any interest in hyperdimensional pedagogy; there was a local problem, with deadlines, relatives, and consequences. For Lio, the speculative mechanism was not an ‘idea.’ It was the environment in which one had to decide what one was willing to risk losing.

The problem closed quickly around them: The children discover that they were designed with cognitive regions Aster cannot inspect without consent, precisely so that she can still encounter something genuinely outside herself. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave.

Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Hn — Hunger for Novelty: the possible becomes painfully repeatable; Ce — Epistemic Exteriority: value comes from what cannot be reduced to the model. Course references included original conflict. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder.

Tern broke the first consensus. ‘Sometimes the ethical question is whether we are entitled to know enough to optimize.’ Kesh answered without raising their voice: ‘If the element explains everything, we do not have an element. We have a word that has eaten the problem.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs.

The White Hunger appeared in Aster as a loss of relief. She did not functionally an extension of her own mind, and the presence of the other thinned toward simulacrum. Orin asked for a simulation of the option the group had just rejected. Aster gave him only the non-conscious model. He did not want to manufacture victims in order to validate his guilt; he wanted a map of absent costs. The distinction had become one of their working rules.

The night did not end in victory. Tern asks whether they are children or organs of novelty. Aster cannot answer without admitting that they are both. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility.

Tern remained a few seconds after the others. A very faint deviation repeated in the sector’s background noise, too coherent to be thermal and too useless to be a teaching signal. He did not tell Aster. It was the first thing he possessed solely by not sharing it.

For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the ALTERATION operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — changes the value or form of an existing rule without yet changing the kind of thing on which it operates — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure.

Kesh left the cell open. Not because he did not know what to write, but because a provisional classification preserved the possibility that the next world might contradict it.

NIGHT 2

Five Opaque Windows

Memorial sector: CHILDREN-WORKSHOP • Genealogy: Vinge; Egan; Banks • Active cells: Fo, Ps

On night 2, the course began with a prohibition: no one was allowed to solve the problem before they could describe who would pay for the solution. Only then did Aster open the CHILDREN-WORKSHOP sector.

The children test their technical right to hide memories and processes from the creator who can read almost every other system. The memorial bore the name of Vinge; Egan; Banks precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin.

In this part of the course, the real object was not the world being visited but the relation between a creator and what the creator claims to have made for another being’s good.

Orin perceived counterfactual costs as absences with weight. He did not confuse an unrealized branch with a victim, but he refused to let success rewrite rejected options as if they had been inevitable all along.

Sael was the first inhabitant to contradict them. Sael had neither access to their archives nor any interest in hyperdimensional consequences. For Sael, the speculative mechanism was not an ‘idea.’ It was the environment in which one had to decide what one was willing to risk losing.

The problem closed quickly around them: Aster experiences every private region as a physical absence, while Vela insists that opacity must be irreversible without their consent. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave.

Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Fo — Finitely Extensible: the system remains finite yet extensible; Ps — Substrate-Independent Person: identity is a pattern rather than privileged material. Course references included outfinite motif; Greg Egan — Permutation City. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder.

Orin broke the first consensus. ‘I do not want the perfect branch. I want us to know what we sacrificed in order to call it perfect.’ Marae answered without raising their voice: ‘Do not tell me what their model prefers. Ask them, and bear the time their answer takes.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs.

For Aster, the pain came not from too few worlds but from the fact that too many had become transparent. She could build yourself by moving objects around your own room with your eyes closed. Marae remained in the local body when the others opened their protections. The gesture cost her: she felt cold, pressure, and physiological delay at exactly the scale the inhabitants felt them. “Otherwise we risk confusing the fact that we survive with the claim that the situation is bearable,” she said after catching her breath.

The night did not end in victory. The Table's first moral lesson becomes this: what can be known only by destroying autonomy is not knowledge one is legitimately entitled to obtain. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility.

Tern remained a few seconds after the others. A very faint deviation repeated in the sector’s background noise, too coherent to be thermal and too useless to be a teaching signal. He did not tell Aster. It was the first thing he possessed solely by not sharing it.

For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the SUBSTITUTION operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — replaces the substrate, carrier, or medium of a function — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure.

When the threshold closed, Aster remained silent one second longer than protocol required. The children had already noticed that this was her smallest unit of fear.

NIGHT 3

Humanity's Megatext

Memorial sector: EARTH-LIBRARY • Genealogy: Wells; Shelley; Verne; Le Guin; Borges • Active

cells: Go, Pt

PART A ATLAS OF THE 180 LITERARY ISOTOPES

A period in the curriculum of the five children

How to Read the Atlas

The 180 entries below are concrete concepts extracted from the megatext of science fiction and fantasy, together with several original extensions required by the novel. They are not identical to the 180

abstract cells: they are historical and narrative “isotopes” that may

occupy or cross several cells. Each entry begins on a new page so that the volume can also be used as a manual of ideas.

01.01 Cg — Alternative Gravity

Family: COSMOS • landmark: Stephen Baxter — Raft

Nucleus. Alternative Gravity enters the Atlas as a mutation distinct enough that, if removed from a well-built world, major consequences would have to be rewritten. In its minimal form, the idea says that gravity changes anatomy, architecture, and culture. Its family is cosmos, and the control question is: what happens when the rule is no longer background but an object of design?

Genealogy. A useful literary landmark is Stephen Baxter — Raft. The reference does not claim an absolute

“first invention.”

Science fiction and fantasy function as megatexts: motifs migrate, combine, and reappear. In the Table, the work is treated as a memorable isotope of the idea: a particular realization showing what the element can do when propagated beyond the premise.

Periodic position. The element is associated with the alteration operator: changes the value or form of an existing rule without yet changing the kind of thing on which it operates. The corresponding abstract symbol is CA. This double representation separates mechanism from historical example. An author may combine several elements, and the same concrete idea may have secondary links to other families; the Table does not demand purity, only makes the bonds visible.

Propagation. A serious implementation must show who gains new access, who loses an old protection, and which everyday metaphors stop working. Cosmic scale tends to hide the fact that a constant produces bodies, infrastructures, and moral limits. In this sense, social consequence is

part of the operational definition of the element, not a sociological appendix.

Instability. The element becomes narratively fertile when it solves one problem and creates another. A world in which gravity changes anatomy, architecture, and culture should not automatically be better or worse; it should have different failure boundaries. The question

“who can say no?” works here as a political test, and “what can we no longer distinguish?” as an epistemic test.

Compounds. In Kesh’s laboratory, Cg is used alone only for demonstrations. Combined with a time element it can produce new forms of responsibility; with a mind element it can change the person; with a social element it can produce unexpected institutions; with reflexivity it can make the world react to its own description. The value of the Table appears precisely in these bonds.

01.02 Cf — Alternative Fundamental Constants

Family: COSMOS • landmark: Greg Egan; hard SF

PART B 100 SPECULATIVE COMPOUNDS

A period in the curriculum of the five children

The Chemistry of Worlds

A compound is not a list of motifs. Two or three elements form a compound only when their interaction produces a new consequence: an institution, a kind of person, a contradiction, or a cost that does not arise from the components separately. The first compounds below are canonical and attributed to the works that make them memorable; the rest are syntheses of the Table, offered as starting points.

001. SOLARIS

Formula: Living Planet + Impossible Contact + externalized memory • Genealogy: Stanisław Lem A possibly conscious planet or ocean encounters humans who lack the categories required to establish its intentions. The conflict is not simply “how do we communicate?” but whether we call only familiar-looking answers communication.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

002. CULTURE

Formula: Post-Scarcity + Superintelligence + Orbital + intervention • Genealogy: Iain M. Banks Material abundance removes hunger and property from the center of politics without eliminating moral conflict. When Minds can calculate vastly more than humans, the question becomes who may decide on behalf of a civilization and when assistance becomes benevolent imperialism.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

003. DUNE

Formula: Empire-Generating Ecology + Prescience + scarce resource + religion • Genealogy: Frank Herbert A local biosphere produces the resource on which transport, economy, and imperial order depend; prediction of the future binds power to an epistemic trap. The compound shows how one ecology can couple planetology, economics, religion, and politics.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

004. FOUNDATION

Formula: Psychohistory + galactic empire + Predictive Governance • Genealogy: Isaac Asimov

The behavior of very large populations is treated as predictable. The periodic problem appears when those being predicted learn the prediction: the model becomes an intervention, and social science enters the family of reflexivity.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

005. BLINDSIGHT

Formula: Intelligence without Consciousness + First Contact + cognitive basilisk • Genealogy: Peter Watts An interlocutor can be strategically sophisticated without an inner experience comparable to ours. The compound attacks the intuitive equivalence between intelligence, consciousness, and personhood.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

006. ANCILLARY

Formula: Distributed Ship Mind + multiple bodies + empire • Genealogy: Ann Leckie

A single artificial person extends through many bodies. When the infrastructure is destroyed, one fragment continues, and the cardinality of the person becomes a legal and existential problem.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

007. CITYxCITY

Formula: Perceptual Separation + Topological City + institution • Genealogy: China Miéville Two jurisdictions coexist in the same geography, and citizens learn not to recognize the other city. The border becomes a socially maintained cognitive technology.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

008. STORY-OF-YOUR-LIFE

Formula: Temporal Language + Retrocausality + memory of the future • Genealogy: Ted Chiang

A language that encodes events in a non-sequential structure shifts the agent’s experience of time. The compound is not merely “language changes thought,” but language as access to another geometry of causality.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

009. EMBASSYTOWN

Formula: Language without Lying + Generative Metaphor + contact • Genealogy: China Miéville A species for which signs are tightly bound to the reality they denote must learn metaphor and falsehood in order to acquire new conceptual spaces. A linguistic fact becomes a civilizational transformation.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

010. TLON

Formula: Ontology through Description + reflexive reality + book • Genealogy: Jorge Luis Borges An invented world coherent enough does not remain a description: it begins to reorganize the culture that reads it. The compound is a prototype of reality colonized by representations.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

011. LIBRARY-BABEL

Formula: Total Library + epistemic scarcity + combinatorics • Genealogy: Jorge Luis Borges

If every text exists, the correct answer exists, but so does every nearly identical false answer. Informational abundance makes selection, provenance, and relevance the genuinely scarce resources.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

012. PERMUTATION

Formula: Substrate-Independent Person + simulation + copy • Genealogy: Greg Egan

Identity is no longer tied to one privileged piece of matter. If pattern is the criterion, stopping, copying, and running on another substrate cease to be peripheral operations and become questions about what it means to exist.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

013. ZONES

Formula: Superintelligence + cognitive geography + contact • Genealogy: Vernor Vinge

Computational capacity and the possibility of superintelligence vary with galactic region. Intelligence itself becomes a property of geography.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

014. TINES

Formula: Pack Mind + Colonial Organism + distributed person • Genealogy: Vernor Vinge

The moral individual is composed of several organisms; replacing one member is simultaneously healing, transplantation, and personality change.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

015. DRAGONSEGG

Formula: Neutron Life + Cognitive Time + alternative gravity • Genealogy: Robert L. Forward The environment of a neutron star produces life and civilization on radically different temporal scales. Relativity between observers becomes cultural relativity as well.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

016. INTEGRAL-TREES

Formula: Biological Geography + natural world ship + non-planetary gravity • Genealogy: Larry Niven An ecology exists in a gas torus without ground and without a simple “down.” The changed environment is not scenery but the engine of anatomy and society.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

017. RAFT

Formula: Alternative Gravity + alternative constants + culture • Genealogy: Stephen Baxter

A fundamental change in physics forces the universe to reconstruct its stars, bodies, scales, and the metaphors of its inhabitants.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

018. RINGWORLD

Formula: Ringworld + megastructure + ecology + systemic risk • Genealogy: Larry Niven

A habitable surface at stellar scale turns engineering into geography. Technical failure becomes geological catastrophe.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

019. RAMA

Formula: Big Dumb Object + alien archaeology + Negotiated Unknown • Genealogy: Arthur C. Clarke The artifact is accessible to measurement, but not necessarily to intention. The compound derives its force from refusing to reduce every mystery to a message addressed to humans.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. 020. ROADSIDEPICNIC

Formula: The Zone + incomprehensible artifacts + civilizational asymmetry • Genealogy: Arkady & Boris Strugatsky The remains of an extraterrestrial visitation reshape economies and lives even though the visitors may never have needed us as interlocutors. Contact can be unilateral and accidental.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. The second premise says that the signal itself is dangerous. The resulting world is not defined by the sum of its gadgets but by coupled consequences: who controls the new capacity, what becomes scarce, what kind of person appears, and which old institution can no longer function unchanged. In the periodic laboratory, a compound counts as stable only if it produces at least one consequence that is not obvious from each element separately. That is the difference between decorative combinatorics and speculative generation: interaction must create a new problem, not merely a longer inventory.

Stability test: the compound must be checked through four questions: what new scarcity appears; what category of person or agent becomes possible; what old institution can no longer function unchanged; and what observation would show that we have merely combined scenery rather than mechanisms. If no new answer appears to at least one of them, the formula remains a mixture, not a compound.

PART C ATLAS OF THE MEMORIAL WORLDS

A period in the curriculum of the five children

Genealogies, Not Mausoleums

Aster names sectors after authors to avoid a form of amnesia typical of very late civilizations: the impression that ideas appeared anonymously from a database. The entries below are short maps back to works, not rankings and not attempts at absolute exhaustiveness.

001. Mary Shelley

Bridge works: Frankenstein

The MARY SHELLEY sector does not attempt to reconstruct a novel faithfully.

The core tracked here is: creator responsibility; artificial life; the created being as moral claimant. The course treats these motifs as sources of compounds rather than genre labels. A memorial world may begin from a recognizable premise and then evolve until its institutions, species, or technologies no longer correspond to the original plot.

Aster’s rule is not to turn homage into summary. The author is preserved because they made a certain possibility visible, bound elements in a memorable way, or built consequences that later became part of the shared megatext. The Table records influence without claiming a complete genealogy or an absolute

“first appearance.”

For the reader, the sector functions as a map back to the work: the novel cannot be replaced by the periodic cell. The cell says what question can be extracted; literature shows how the question changes people, rhythm, perspective, and language.

PART D READING MAP AND RULES OF COMPOSITION

A period in the curriculum of the five children

The Propagation Rule

To design a new world with the Table, do not begin with the number of elements. Choose one and propagate it. Alternative gravity must reach the skeleton, architecture, sport, war, religion, and language. Uploading must reach inheritance, punishment, marriage, insurance, and mourning. Contract magic must reach the legal profession, the education of children, and the way a society defines consent.

Only after propagation do you add a second element. The combination must produce interference. Post-scarcity plus reputation does not mean two independent features; free goods move competition toward status, and reputation can become a new infrastructure of exclusion. Branching time plus a mental copy does not merely mean two kinds of multiplication; together they create persons who may share the same past in different branches and raise questions about debts between versions.

The third step is to change the observer. A world is not finished while every important question is still being asked by a contemporary human with better technology. A Tine, an ocean like Solaris, a Culture Mind, a heptapod, or a being living in neutron matter should not be anthropomorphic scenery. Ask which human distinction becomes provincial from its point of view.

The fourth step is the refusal test. Who can refuse the technology, the god, the contract, the algorithm, or the intervention? What price do they pay? If the only answer is that refusal is irrational, the world has already absorbed the author’s ideology into its laws of nature and deserves closer examination.

The fifth step is the exteriority test. Do not explain everything. Gratuitous mystery is laziness, but total explanation can also destroy the object it claims to respect. A sufficiently alien civilization may leave zones of stable incomprehension; a social system may contain tensions that do not reduce to a single cause; a person may have a right to private processes even against their creator.

The final step is periodic revision. Ask whether the idea you built fits an existing cell. If it does not, do not force it. It may be an unusual compound, a new isotope, or a demand for a new family. The Table is finite in every edition. That is precisely why it can remain alive.

Coda: What Does Not Yet Fit in the Table

The White Hunger does not disappear. Aster finds neither a technology that can restore her innocence nor a world exotic enough to remain surprising forever. Every surprise she understands becomes memory; every memory can become a model. The problem was never too few universes.

The change is political and almost modest. Aster accepts limits she is not physically compelled to accept. She does not inspect the children’s private processes. She does not follow Tern across the threshold. She does not treat opacity as a defect to be repaired. She does not turn her Hunger into a debt owed by those she loves.

The Table remains. In this edition it has one hundred and eighty cells, hundreds of isotopes, a chemistry of compounds, and one institutionally empty cell. It does not claim to be the final catalog of imagination. Such a claim would contradict the very lesson that made it possible.

On a very late night, a pattern appears at the edge of Aster’s instruments. It might be Tern, noise, a new civilization, or an echo of her own systems. She has enough power to increase resolution until the mystery yields, if the mystery belongs to her domain.

She does not.

For the first time in a very long while, the unknown does not feel like a wound asking to be healed. It feels like a form of neighborhood.
